title: 22. Interview: Cache Eviction
summary: Interview Q&A for Cache Eviction — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Cache Eviction interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is cache eviction, and why is the policy choice important?
**Answer:** Cache eviction is the algorithm that decides which entries to remove when the cache is full and a new entry must be admitted. Every bounded cache must evict (memory is finite, working sets are larger than caches), and the eviction policy is what determines whether the cache holds the "right" entries — the ones that will be re-accessed — or fills with cold data. The policy choice can swing hit rate from 30% to 95% on the same workload, directly translating to database load, latency, and cost. The wrong policy on a scan-heavy workload can effectively disable the cache (LRU evicts hot keys when a scan pollutes the cache, dropping hit rate from 80% to 30%); the right policy (LFU or W-TinyLFU) keeps the hot working set resident despite scans. Real-world: Redis exposes `maxmemory-policy` with eight options; the choice between `allkeys-lru` and `allkeys-lfu` depends entirely on the workload's access pattern. Caffeine defaults to W-TinyLFU because it achieves the best hit rate on the widest range of workloads.
**Visual:**
```
Cache full, new key arrives:
  + which entry to evict?  -> policy decides
  + right policy:  hot working set stays -> 95% hit rate
  + wrong policy:  cold data displaces hot -> 30% hit rate

Impact: 30% vs 95% hit rate = 65% more DB load = 5x more DB cost
```

### Q2. Compare LRU and LFU. When does each win?
**Answer:** LRU evicts the entry accessed least recently; LFU evicts the entry with the lowest access count. LRU wins on workloads with **temporal locality** (recently accessed keys are likely to be re-accessed soon — session data, recently-viewed lists) and on workloads with **shifting hot keys** (the hot set changes over time, and LRU adapts within a few cache-misses). LFU wins on workloads with **stable hot keys** (a small set of keys is hot for a long time — product catalogs, popular videos) and on **scan-heavy workloads** (LRU is demolished by scans; LFU is scan-resistant because one-time scans don't accumulate enough count to evict high-frequency keys). LRU's weakness: scan pollution — a long sequential read evicts the hot working set. LFU's weakness: slow adaptation — a key that was hot yesterday but cold today keeps its high count for a long time, occupying space that should go to new hot keys. Real-world: Redis `allkeys-lru` for general workloads with shifting hot keys; `allkeys-lfu` for stable hot keys with occasional scans (e.g., a product catalog crawled by a search bot). Modern systems often use W-TinyLFU, which combines the best of both.
**Visual:**
```
Workload                  Best policy   Reason
------------------------  -----------   ------------------------------
temporal locality         LRU           recent predicts future
shifting hot keys         LRU           adapts fast to shifts
stable hot keys           LFU           frequency is strong predictor
scan-heavy                LFU           scan-resistant (low count)
mixed (real-world)        W-TinyLFU     combines recency + frequency
```

### Q3. What is scan pollution, and how does it affect LRU?
**Answer:** Scan pollution occurs when a long sequential read of cold keys displaces the hot working set from the cache. Each scanned key is "more recently used" than the previous hot keys (because LRU updates recency on access), so a full scan of N cold keys evicts up to N hot keys, even though the scanned keys will never be re-accessed. After the scan, the cache is full of cold data, and the next request for a hot key misses — hit rate collapses until the hot keys are re-loaded. Example: a 1000-key cache with a 100-key hot working set (95% hit rate); a backup job scans 100,000 cold keys; after the scan, the cache holds 1000 cold keys and 0 hot keys; hit rate drops to 0% until the hot keys are re-accessed and re-loaded. LRU's lack of scan resistance is its biggest weakness; LFU and W-TinyLFU are scan-resistant because one-time scans don't accumulate enough frequency to evict high-frequency hot keys. Real-world: a periodic crawler on a product catalog (Amazon, eBay) will scan thousands of product pages; with LRU, the hot products get evicted; with LFU or W-TinyLFU, the hot products stay.
**Visual:**
```
Before scan: cache has 100 hot keys (95% hit rate)
  [H1][H2][H3]...[H100]   (hot working set resident)

Scan of 1000 cold keys (C1..C1000):
  LRU evicts hot keys to make room for cold:
  [C901][C902]...[C1000]   (cache full of cold, hot evicted)

After scan: hot key request -> MISS (cache has cold data, not hot)
  hit rate: 0% until hot keys are re-loaded

LFU/W-TinyLFU: scan keys have low freq -> rejected at admission
  hot keys stay resident, scan doesn't pollute
```

### Q4. What is W-TinyLFU, and why does Caffeine use it?
**Answer:** W-TinyLFU is a modern eviction policy that combines a small windowed LRU (1% of capacity, for recency) with a main space governed by TinyLFU admission control (80% probationary, 20% protected, for frequency). When the window LRU fills and a candidate must be promoted to the main space, TinyLFU compares the candidate's estimated frequency against the victim's frequency; the candidate is admitted only if higher. The frequency estimator is a **Count-Min Sketch** with aging — a probabilistic data structure with sub-byte counters that decays old counts over time, allowing adaptation to access pattern shifts. W-TinyLFU wins because: (1) It's scan-resistant — one-time scans don't accumulate enough frequency to be admitted. (2) It adapts to shifts — the aging sketch forgets old frequencies, so previously-hot keys lose their priority. (3) It captures recency — the window LRU handles bursty short-term patterns. (4) It achieves hit rates within 1% of the theoretical optimum (Belady's MIN) on most workloads. Caffeine (used by Netflix, Uber, Spring Boot) defaults to W-TinyLFU because it dominates LRU and LFU on the widest range of real-world workloads. Real-world: Redis 4.0+ added an LFU mode inspired by similar ideas; Hazelcast and Apache Ignite also use W-TinyLFU.
**Visual:**
```
W-TinyLFU cache layout:
  +----------------+------------+---------------+
  | Window LRU 1%  | Probation  | Protected 20% |
  | (recency)      | 80%        | (frequency)   |
  +----------------+------------+---------------+

New key -> window LRU
  when window full -> candidate for main space
  TinyLFU: admit only if candidate_freq > victim_freq
  (frequencies from Count-Min Sketch with aging)

Result:
  + scan-resistant (one-time scans have low freq)
  + adapts to shifts (sketch ages, old freqs decay)
  + captures recency (window LRU)
  + within 1% of optimal (Belady's MIN) on most workloads
```

### Q5. What is Redis's approximate LRU, and why does Redis use it instead of true LRU?
**Answer:** Redis's `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` does not implement true LRU (a global doubly-linked list moved on every access) — it implements **approximate LRU**: when eviction is needed, Redis samples N keys (controlled by `maxmemory-samples`, default 5) and evicts the least recently used among the sample. The approximation is within a few percent of true LRU's hit rate but is much cheaper: (1) No global linked list to update under a lock on every access — concurrent throughput is higher. (2) No per-key linked-list pointers — memory overhead is lower. (3) The sample size is tunable — `maxmemory-samples 10` gets closer to true LRU at higher CPU cost. Redis uses approximate LRU because true LRU's lock contention on the global list would be a bottleneck at Redis's typical throughput (hundreds of thousands of ops/sec per instance). The same logic applies to Redis's approximate LFU — it samples N keys and picks the lowest frequency. Real-world: most production Redis deployments use the default `maxmemory-samples 5`; operators who need closer-to-true-LRU behavior bump it to 10. The trade-off is well-documented in Redis's `redis.conf`.
**Visual:**
```
True LRU:           global linked list, move-to-head on every access
                     + lock contention, O(1) but serializing
Approximate LRU:    sample N keys, evict LRU among sample
                     + no global list, no lock contention
                     + within ~5% of true LRU hit rate

maxmemory-samples=5  (default, ~5% deviation)
maxmemory-samples=10 (closer to true LRU, ~2% deviation, more CPU)
```

### Q6. What is ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache), and how does it self-tune?
**Answer:** ARC maintains two lists: T1 (recently used once — recency-based) and T2 (used more than once — frequency-based), plus two ghost lists B1 and B2 (recently evicted from T1 and T2, respectively, tracking metadata only). The boundary `p` between T1 and T2's target sizes adapts: if a request hits B1 (a key recently evicted from T1 would have been useful), ARC increases `p` (favoring recency); if a request hits B2 (a key recently evicted from T2 would have been useful), ARC decreases `p` (favoring frequency). The ghost lists provide the feedback signal — they tell ARC "your last eviction from T1 (or T2) was wrong; rebalance." This self-tuning means ARC automatically adapts to the workload without manual policy selection: on a recency-heavy workload, ARC shifts toward LRU; on a frequency-heavy workload, ARC shifts toward LFU. ARC's weakness is complexity — the four lists and the adaptation logic are harder to implement and debug than LRU or LFU. ARC is used in ZFS's ARC (the name is from the algorithm), IBM DB2, and some storage caches. Real-world: ZFS's ARC is the best-known deployment; it adapts to the workload's mix of sequential and random access without operator tuning.
**Visual:**
```
ARC cache:
  T1 (recently used)  |  T2 (frequently used)
  <----- p target ---->  <--- capacity - p --->
       (recency)              (frequency)

  Ghost lists: B1 (evicted from T1), B2 (evicted from T2)

Hit on B1:  ARC was wrong to evict from T1 -> increase p (favor recency)
Hit on B2:  ARC was wrong to evict from T2 -> decrease p (favor frequency)

Self-tunes: shifts toward LRU on recency workloads, LFU on frequency workloads
```

### Q7. How do you choose an eviction policy for a production cache?
**Answer:** Start by **measuring the access pattern**: collect a sample of cache requests (a few million) and compute (1) the Zipf skew (what fraction of accesses go to the top 1% of keys), (2) the scan frequency (how often a long sequential read occurs), (3) the hot-key churn rate (how often the hot set changes). Then **simulate policies offline**: run LRU, LFU, FIFO, Random, and W-TinyLFU on the sampled trace and compare hit rates. Choose the policy with the best hit rate on the trace, with a bias toward W-TinyLFU (which is robust across patterns) unless you have a specific reason (e.g., lock-free concurrency favoring Random). For **Redis**, set `maxmemory-policy` based on the workload: `allkeys-lru` for general, `allkeys-lfu` for stable hot keys with scans, `volatile-ttl` for TTL-based eviction (e.g., session caches where shorter TTL = more disposable). For **in-process caches** (Caffeine, Guava), use W-TinyLFU (Caffeine default) unless you have a strong reason. Always **monitor hit rate in production** — if it drops below the simulated expectation, investigate (workload shift, cache undersized, scan pollution). Real-world: Netflix measures hit rate on every cache and alerts if it drops below 90% (their SLO); Amazon's product cache was historically LRU but moved to LFU-like policies as the catalog grew and hot products stabilized.
**Visual:**
```
Decision tree:
  1. Sample production traffic (1M requests)
  2. Compute: Zipf skew, scan freq, hot-key churn
  3. Simulate: LRU, LFU, FIFO, Random, W-TinyLFU on the trace
  4. Pick best hit rate (bias toward W-TinyLFU for robustness)
  5. Deploy; monitor hit rate in production
  6. Alert if hit rate < SLO (e.g., 90%)

Redis-specific:
  + general workload          -> allkeys-lru
  + stable hot keys + scans   -> allkeys-lfu
  + session cache with TTL    -> volatile-ttl
  + don't evict (return err)  -> noeviction (write-heavy, must not lose)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your Redis cache has a 95% hit rate during the day but drops to 60% at midnight. The midnight drop coincides with a nightly backup job that scans all keys. What's happening, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The backup job is causing **scan pollution** — it sequentially reads every key, and Redis's `allkeys-lru` policy treats each scanned key as "recently used," evicting the hot working set to make room for cold backup-scanned keys. After the backup completes, the cache is full of cold data, and the next wave of normal traffic misses the hot keys, dropping hit rate to 60% until the hot keys are re-loaded. Fixes: (1) **Change the eviction policy** to `allkeys-lfu` — LFU is scan-resistant because one-time scans don't accumulate enough count to evict high-frequency keys; the hot working set stays resident despite the backup. (2) **Use a separate cache or DB replica for the backup** — the backup reads from a read-replica of the database, not from the cache, so it doesn't pollute the cache. (3) **Throttle the backup** — slow it down so it doesn't read faster than the cache can absorb (but this doesn't fix the underlying pollution). (4) **Skip the cache for backup reads** — modify the backup tool to bypass the cache (e.g., Redis `SCAN` with `NOTOUCH` flag if available, or read directly from the DB). The best fix depends on the architecture: if the cache is the source of truth (write-back), use option 1 (LFU); if the DB is the source of truth, use option 2 (backup from replica). Real-world: this is a common Redis operational issue; many teams discover LFU specifically because of backup-scan pollution.
**Visual:**
```
Daytime (no backup):
  cache: [hot1][hot2]...[hot1000] (working set resident)
  hit rate: 95%

Midnight backup scans 1M keys:
  LRU evicts hot keys to admit scanned keys:
  cache: [scan1][scan2]...[scan1000] (cold, will never be re-accessed)
  hot keys evicted -> next traffic wave: 60% hit rate

Fix: switch to allkeys-lfu
  scan keys have low freq -> not admitted (rejected at eviction time)
  hot keys stay resident -> hit rate stays 95% during backup
```

### Q2. You're caching Instagram user profiles. The hot set (top 1% of users) accounts for 80% of traffic, but the hot set shifts weekly as new users go viral. Which eviction policy do you choose?
**Answer:** This is a workload with **stable skew but shifting hot keys** — frequency is a strong predictor within a week, but the hot set changes week-to-week. Pure LFU would be too slow to adapt — a user who was hot last week but cold this week keeps a high frequency count for a long time, occupying space that should go to new hot users. Pure LRU would adapt to shifts but is vulnerable to scan pollution (e.g., a crawler reading profile pages). The best choice is **W-TinyLFU** (Caffeine) or **Redis `allkeys-lfu` with frequency aging** (Redis 4.0+ LFU has a `lfu-decay-time` parameter that ages counts over time). The aging mechanism is key: it gradually decays old frequencies, so last-week's hot users lose priority as this-week's hot users accumulate count. If using Redis, set `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu` and `lfu-decay-time 1` (decay counter by 1 every minute); if using Caffeine in-process, the default W-TinyLFU aging is already appropriate. Monitor hit rate weekly — if it drops, the decay time may need tuning (faster decay for faster-shifting hot sets). Real-world: Instagram, TikTok, and Twitter all face this pattern; modern in-process caches use W-TinyLFU specifically because of its aging adaptation.
**Visual:**
```
Workload:
  + 1% of users = 80% of traffic (Zipf skew, stable)
  + hot set shifts weekly (new viral users)

LFU (no aging):    last week's hot users keep high count
                  -> this week's hot users can't displace them
                  -> hit rate drops as shift accumulates

LRU:               adapts to shifts within a few cache-misses
                  -> but vulnerable to scan pollution (crawler)

W-TinyLFU (best):  frequency with aging
                  -> last week's hot users decay, this week's accumulate
                  -> scan-resistant + shift-adaptive
```

### Q3. Your team is using a cache with FIFO eviction. Hit rate is 40%, but your SLO is 80%. The workload is read-heavy with a stable hot set. Why is FIFO underperforming, and what do you switch to?
**Answer:** FIFO is underperforming because it ignores access pattern entirely — it evicts the oldest *admitted* entry, regardless of how often it's been accessed since admission. On a stable hot set, the hot keys are accessed frequently and should stay resident, but FIFO evicts them when they reach the front of the admission queue, even if they were accessed 1000 times. This is fundamentally wrong for a hot-set workload. Switch to **LRU** (if no scans) or **LFU / W-TinyLFU** (if scans are present). For a stable hot set with no scans, LRU will give ~80–90% hit rate (hot keys are "recently used" so they stay at the head of the recency list). For a stable hot set with occasional scans (e.g., a crawler), LFU or W-TinyLFU will give ~85–95% hit rate (scan-resistant, hot keys stay resident by frequency). The expected jump from 40% (FIFO) to 85%+ (LRU/LFU) is dramatic — FIFO is essentially never the right choice for a hot-set workload. Real-world: FIFO is used in write-ahead log buffers (where write order is meaningful) but almost never in read caches; if you find FIFO in a read cache, it's usually a mistake. Switch to LRU as a safe default, or W-TinyLFU for the best hit rate.
**Visual:**
```
FIFO on hot-set workload:
  admission order:  [k1][k2][hot][k4][k5]...
  access pattern:    hot accessed 1000x, others 1x
  eviction:          evict k1 (oldest admitted), then k2, then hot (!)
                    -> hot evicted despite 1000 accesses
  hit rate: 40% (hot constantly evicted and re-loaded)

LRU on same workload:
  recency order:     [k4][k5][hot][k2][k1]...  (hot moved to head)
  eviction:          evict k1 (least recently used), hot stays
  hit rate: 85% (hot stays resident)

Switch: FIFO -> LRU (or W-TinyLFU for scan resistance)
```

### Q4. Your Kafka consumer group uses an in-memory cache for deduplicating messages (idempotency keys). The cache is bounded at 1M entries. Which eviction policy minimizes duplicate processing?
**Answer:** For idempotency deduplication, the goal is to maximize the probability that a recently-seen key is still in the cache when (and if) a duplicate arrives. The access pattern is: each key is written once on first delivery, then potentially read on redelivery (if Kafka retries). Most keys are never redelivered; a small fraction (the duplicates) are read. This is a **temporal locality** workload — duplicates tend to arrive shortly after the first delivery (within Kafka's retry interval, typically seconds to minutes). The best policy is **LRU** with a TTL matching the Kafka retry interval (e.g., 10 minutes): (1) LRU keeps the most recently seen keys resident, which are the most likely to be redelivered (since duplicates cluster temporally). (2) The TTL bounds memory usage and ensures the cache doesn't hold keys older than the retry interval (which would never be redelivered). (3) LFU would be wrong — most keys have frequency 1 (no duplicate), so LFU would have no signal to differentiate; LRU's recency signal is what matters. (4) W-TinyLFU would also work but is overkill for this pattern. Real-world: Kafka consumer idempotency often uses a TTL-bounded LRU (or a time-windowed cache like a sliding window of seen keys); Spark Structured Streaming uses a similar pattern for exactly-once deduplication.
**Visual:**
```
Idempotency cache access pattern:
  + write each key once (first delivery)
  + read small fraction (duplicates, within retry interval)
  + temporal locality: duplicates arrive shortly after first

Best policy: LRU + TTL
  LRU: keeps recently-seen keys (most likely duplicates)
  TTL: bounds memory, expires keys older than retry interval

Wrong policy: LFU
  most keys have freq=1 -> no signal to differentiate
  would evict randomly among freq=1 keys
```

### Q5. You're using Caffeine (W-TinyLFU) for an in-process cache in a Java service. The hit rate is 92%, but you've noticed it drops to 70% during marketing campaigns that drive a flood of new users. Why, and what do you do?
**Answer:** Marketing campaigns drive a flood of accesses to **new keys** (new user profiles, new product pages) that aren't yet in the cache's frequency sketch. W-TinyLFU's admission control compares the candidate's frequency (from the Count-Min Sketch) against the victim's frequency; new keys have frequency 0 (or 1, after first access), so they're rejected at admission in favor of existing entries with higher frequency. This is usually good (scan-resistant), but during a campaign, the new keys are *legitimately* hot — they should be admitted — but W-TinyLFU's conservative admission rejects them, dropping hit rate. Fixes: (1) **Increase the window LRU size** — Caffeine exposes this; a larger window admits more new entries based on recency alone, before frequency-based admission kicks in. (2) **Pre-warm the cache** — when a campaign starts, pre-load the new hot keys (e.g., from a list of campaign products) so they bypass the admission filter. (3) **Increase the cache capacity during campaigns** — auto-scale the cache size to absorb the burst; the frequency sketch will catch up as accesses accumulate. (4) **Accept the temporary drop** — 70% is still acceptable; once the campaign stabilizes, the new keys accumulate frequency and hit rate recovers to 92%. Real-world: Netflix pre-warms caches for new show launches; Amazon pre-warms product caches for Prime Day. The lesson: W-TinyLFU's strength (scan resistance) is also its weakness when the "scan" is actually legitimate new traffic.
**Visual:**
```
Normal operation:
  + hot keys have high freq in sketch -> admitted on eviction
  + new keys have low freq -> rejected (scan resistance)
  + hit rate: 92%

Marketing campaign (flood of new users):
  + new keys are legitimately hot but have low freq
  + W-TinyLFU rejects them (treats as scan)
  + hit rate: 70% (new keys can't get admitted)

Fixes:
  + pre-warm cache with campaign keys (bypass admission)
  + increase window LRU size (more recency-based admission)
  + auto-scale capacity during campaigns
  + accept temporary drop (recovers as freq accumulates)
```

### Q6. Your team is using Redis with `maxmemory-policy noeviction` (return errors when full) for a session cache. The cache is filling up and you're seeing errors. What are your options?
**Answer:** `noeviction` means Redis returns an error on writes when `maxmemory` is reached, rather than evicting — this is appropriate when data loss is unacceptable, but it requires careful capacity planning. Options: (1) **Increase `maxmemory`** — if the server has more RAM, raise the limit; the simplest fix if the working set just grew. (2) **Switch to `volatile-lru` or `volatile-ttl`** — evict only among keys with a TTL set; sessions have TTLs (e.g., 30 minutes), so this evicts expired-soon sessions to make room, never touching TTL-less keys (which might be more important). (3) **Switch to `allkeys-lru`** — evict the least recently used entry regardless of TTL; this is appropriate if all keys are session-like (short-lived) and you don't distinguish TTL'd from non-TTL'd. (4) **Reduce TTLs** — if sessions currently expire after 30 minutes, reducing to 10 minutes frees space faster; the trade-off is users get logged out sooner. (5) **Shard the cache** — distribute sessions across multiple Redis instances (Redis Cluster), increasing total capacity. (6) **Move cold sessions to disk** — tier sessions to a disk-backed store (e.g., Redis on SSD, or a separate key-value store like RocksDB) after they're idle for some time. For a session cache, option 2 (`volatile-lru`) or 3 (`allkeys-lru`) is usually best — sessions are short-lived and eviction is acceptable (the user just re-logs in). `noeviction` is wrong for session caches because sessions are inherently disposable. Real-world: most Redis session caches use `volatile-lru` or `allkeys-lru`; `noeviction` is reserved for caches where every key is precious (e.g., a deduplication cache).
**Visual:**
```
noeviction on a session cache (WRONG):
  + cache fills up -> writes return OOM error
  + users can't log in (write fails) -> bad UX

Options:
  + increase maxmemory (if RAM available)
  + switch to volatile-lru (evict expiring-soon sessions)
  + switch to allkeys-lru (evict least-recently-used)
  + reduce TTLs (free space faster, users log out sooner)
  + shard (Redis Cluster, more capacity)
  + tier to disk (cold sessions to SSD)

Best for session cache: volatile-lru or allkeys-lru
  (sessions are disposable, eviction is acceptable)
```

### Q7. You're caching Amazon product pages. The top 1000 products (out of 100M) account for 50% of traffic, but the other 50% is long-tail searches hitting random products. The cache is sized at 10M entries. What eviction policy do you choose, and what hit rate do you expect?
**Answer:** This is a **Zipf-distributed workload with a long tail** — 1000 hot products (50% of traffic) plus 50M cold products (50% of traffic, each accessed rarely). The cache (10M entries) can hold the 1000 hot products plus 9.999M cold products. The optimal policy: (1) **Always keep the 1000 hot products resident** — they generate 50% of traffic, so missing them is catastrophic. (2) **Best-effort the long tail** — the other 50% of traffic is spread across 50M products; the cache can hold 9.999M of them (20% of the long tail), so the long-tail hit rate is bounded by 20% × (skew within the tail). Best policy: **W-TinyLFU** (or Redis `allkeys-lfu`) — the 1000 hot products accumulate high frequency and stay resident; the long-tail products compete for the remaining space by frequency, and the ones accessed multiple times (within the tail) are favored over one-time accesses. Expected hit rate: ~50% (hot set) + ~15% (long tail, 20% of 50% adjusted for within-tail skew) = ~65%. LRU would do worse because long-tail accesses pollute the cache (each long-tail access moves the key to the head, potentially evicting a hot product). LFU without aging would do similarly but adapt slower to hot-set shifts. Real-world: Amazon's product cache is reportedly LFU-like with aging, achieving ~70% hit rate on exactly this pattern.
**Visual:**
```
Workload:
  + 1000 hot products: 50% of traffic (each ~50K accesses/day)
  + 50M long-tail:     50% of traffic (each ~1 access/day)
  + cache: 10M entries (1000 hot + 9.999M long-tail)

Optimal: W-TinyLFU / allkeys-lfu
  + hot 1000 stay resident (high freq, never evicted)
  + long-tail: 20% in cache (9.999M / 50M), best-effort by freq

Expected hit rate:
  hot set:   1000/1000 in cache -> 50% of traffic hits cache
  long tail: 20% in cache, ~30% within-tail skew -> ~15% of traffic hits
  total:     ~65% hit rate

LRU would do worse: long-tail accesses pollute, evict hot products
```

LRU wins on workloads with temporal locality (recently accessed keys are likely to be re-accessed soon — session data, recently-viewed lists) and on workloads with shifting hot keys (the hot set changes over time, and LRU adapts within a few cache-misses).

Scan pollution occurs when a long sequential read of cold keys displaces the hot working set from the cache.
quiz.explanation: Scan pollution occurs when a long sequential read of cold keys displaces the hot working set from the cache. Each scanned key is "more recently used" than the previous hot keys (because LRU updates recency on access), so a full scan of N cold keys evicts up to N hot keys, even though the scanned keys will never be re-accessed.

quiz.explanation: W-TinyLFU is a modern eviction policy that combines a small windowed LRU (1% of capacity, for recency) with a main space governed by TinyLFU admission control (80% probationary, 20% protected, for frequency). When the window LRU fills and a candidate must be promoted to the main space, TinyLFU compares the candidate's estimated frequency against the victim's frequency; the candidate is admitted only if higher.

quiz.explanation: Redis's maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru does not implement true LRU (a global doubly-linked list moved on every access) — it implements approximate LRU: when eviction is needed, Redis samples N keys (controlled by maxmemory-samples, default 5) and evicts the least recently used among the sample.
